source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A specific diagnosis pointing to only one particular condition, similar to what the family member is currently assuming this elevated value means","B":"A finding with no clinical relevance whatsoever, contrary to why this particular lab value was actually drawn and is being reviewed","C":"Tissue damage or cell turnover from a variety of causes, rather than pointing to one single specific diagnosis as the family member is currently assuming","D":"Normal, healthy cellular function requiring no follow-up, contrary to what this significantly elevated value actually calls for"}}
source_row.rationale: Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is a nonspecific enzyme marker released from damaged or rapidly turning-over cells, and can be elevated in a variety of conditions, including hemolysis (red blood cell breakdown), tissue injury (such as myocardial infarction or muscle injury), certain cancers (including lymphoma), and some infections, requiring further clinical correlation and additional testing to identify the specific underlying cause.
source_row.source_name: Clinical Laboratory Reference Standards — LDH as a Nonspecific Marker
source_row.stem: A nurse reviews a client's elevated lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) level, and a family member assumes this single number must point toward one very specific diagnosis. The nurse should recognize this as a nonspecific marker that can instead indicate:
